generatedFrom: a development TSA (RFC 3161), via the archive-layer writer of the first implementation
note: These vectors pin the CANONICALISATION TARGET of an archive layer and the way layers are read. The tokens come from a development TSA; that is no objection here, because what must be caught is not whether an authority is trusted but WHAT a layer covers. The trust root ships so the trust path can be walked too.
rules: The input of a layer is the §a.2 canonicalisation up to the opening of the block itself — the same computation a signature's input begins with.
Signatures and layers live in ONE index space. Give them separate numbering and a layer no longer covers the signatures.
A changed byte beneath a layer breaks THAT LAYER, not the signature beneath it. Two claims, two reports.
Nothing in the block is covered by its own token. The comment line is for a human; the token decides.

cases.name: one layer over one signature
cases.note: The simplest form. The layer covers the signature block above it.

cases.name: two layers — the second covers the first
cases.note: Renewal is an ordinary append. That the second layer covers the first is not a special provision but a consequence: the canonicalisation runs up to the block.

cases.name: one layer over a signature with a covers list
cases.note: A covers list sits in the signature block's metadata and therefore inside the layer's coverage. This vector exists to catch a list field shifting the canonicalisation.

cases.name: a damaged layer — and the signature beneath it stays what it was
cases.note: The inserted line falls inside the layer and outside every signature. Two different reports: the archive is not intact, the signer's key stands apart from that (§a.13).
